text:
Hello There! 👋
I’m Federica Domecq, an M.S. in Statistics Student and Teaching Assistant at Wake Forest University. Originally from Madrid, Spain 🇪🇸, I moved to the U.S. to pursue my education and recently graduated from Pomona College with a double major in Mathematics & Computer Science.
On this website you can learn a little bit about me, my research and some of my data wrangling efforts!

title: Fede's Hub
text:
My name is Federica, and I’m a recent graduate of Pomona College, where I double-majored in Mathematics & Computer Science. Originally from Madrid, Spain 🇪🇸, I moved to the U.S. to pursue new opportunities and spent the last four years living in Claremont, California.
Over my time at Pomona, I came to love using data to turn messy problems into clear decisions. My interests sit at the intersection of statistical modeling, optimisation, machine learning, and data visualisation — I enjoy everything from building predictive models to crafting visual stories that make results accessible to everyone.
I’m now at Wake Forest University, pursuing my M.S. in Statistics on a Teaching Assistantship.







Claremont, CA







My Graduation Day







I have spent the past two summers in Pomona College doing some really exciting work alongside some of my favourite Professors, and have continued extending some of that work since graduating:
 2026, Extending On Par Golf: From Proof-of-Concept to Publication
For the past few months, I have been building on the golf strategy project below (On Par, Summer ’25) — a data-driven framework using Gaussian Process Regression to recommend optimal club and aimpoint choices for a golfer based on their own shot tendencies and the course’s layout. Working primarily with Dr. Jo Hardin, we’ve been extending the project with the goal of completing a full manuscript for peer-reviewed publication. This phase has pushed well beyond the original proof-of-concept and has delved further into formalising a multi-fidelity Gaussian Process fusion that combines simulated and real-outcome data for game play simulation. We have run a full convergence analysis to determine how many Monte Carlo samples are needed before a strategy recommendation can be trusted, and have expanded our set of strategy recommendations by providing the user all club-aimpoint combinations that result in statistically indistinguishable outcomes. We have run a broader sensitivity analysis to investigate how changes in player’s shot patterns may independently affect optimal strategy and outcomes, speaking to the long-standing “drive for show, putt for dough” debate in golf analytics. The paper isn’t posted here yet — I’ll share it once it’s finished and submitted (we’re targeting the Journal of Statistics and Data Science in Sports (JSDSS), a fully open-access journal), but wanted to flag that this is very much active, ongoing work. Find out more about this work here.
 2026, Senior Thesis: The Math of Moral Compromise, Beyond Arrow’s Impossibility
For my senior thesis in Mathematics, advised by Dr. Vin de Silva, I explored the mathematics of collective decision-making — why no voting system can ever be perfectly fair. After tracing the history of voting theory from Ancient Greece through the French Revolution to the 20th century, I presented a full combinatorial proof of Arrow’s Impossibility Theorem before introducing a topological approach using ultrafilters, which offers a structurally cleaner explanation for why dictatorship is mathematically unavoidable on any finite electorate. From a topological perspective we can look at what changes (and what doesn’t) under infinite electorates. The thesis closes with a discussion of what all this means for democracy in practice and ways to work around the limitations of this mathematical conundrum. The work was completed with Distinction. Find out more about this work here.




Presenting my Senior Thesis



 Summer ’25, Simulating Golf Strategy using Gaussian Process Regression
During this project we developed a novel data-driven framework to help golfers make better strategic decisions on the course. We modeled golf as a sequential decision-making problem under uncertainty, creating a tool that offers personalized, data-backed recommendations. Using 2D Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), we built a model that assesses the scoring impact of different club and aimpoint combinations. The framework can be tailored to an individual golfer’s tendencies (recorded on Trackman data) and needs, alongside the specific golf course layout, and can be adjusted to either minimise expected strokes (the best score on average) or maximise birdie odds (for high-stakes situations). The work establishes a scalable foundation for a future decision-support tool that provides dynamic, adaptive strategy in real-time based on shot outcomes. I produced this initial work alongside Professor Gabriel Chandler. This project was selected as the national winner (1st Prize) at USRESP and I was given the honour of presenting at eCOTS 2026. Find out more about this work here.
 Summer ’24, Evaluating the Reliability of Sicegar for Timing Analysis of RpoS-Dependent Gene Expression
We used a simulation-based approach to evaluate the sicegar R package, a tool used by biologists to analyse gene expression data. The project focused on assessing whether the package could reliably detect sigmoidal and double-sigmoidal curves and accurately estimate their onset times - the points where gene expression significantly increases and therefore is activated. By generating synthetic data with known parameters and then introducing noise, we tested the software’s performance under various conditions. The results showed that sicegar tends to underestimate the true onset time as data dispersion increases. We then developed a parametric bootstrapping method to correct this bias, demonstrating that this fix can produce estimates that are closer to the real values. I produced this work alongside Professor Jo Hardin. Find out more about this work here.



Every once in a while I participate in tidytuesday, which is a weekly social data project with the opportunity to wrangle analyse and visualise new datasets everyweek. As of the creation of this website, I will start to upload some of my work and process here.



When I’m not working on a problem set or a paper, I’m usually outside — golfing, doing something creative, or, lately, learning pickleball. I like trying new sports and staying active. 
I just finished my collegiate carreer as part of Pomona-Pitzer’s Varsity Women’s Golf team — I served as 2-year Team Captain, made 3 NCAA National appearances, won countless team titles which at one point in time ranked us 1st in the country , and won 2 individual national titles!
I just started a new section on this website dedicated to reflections on my time as a golfer, and dedicated to my very many interests, you can learn more about my interests outside of the classroom here.







On the course with Pomona-Pitzer Golf







A Photo with Some of My Phenomenal Teammates








Tools I feel comfortable with include R, Python, Java, JavaScript, and HTML / SCSS. I use tidyverse-style workflows for data wrangling and visualisation, and I’ve worked with HPC for large simulations, as well as GPyTorch for Gaussian Process modeling.

At this moment in time, I’m starting my M.S. in Statistics at Wake Forest University, while continuing to seek data science / analytics opportunities that combine problem-solving, creativity, and impact. If that sounds like a fit, let’s connect! ✨

title: K-Means Clustering Food Security
text:
This is an unsupervised machine learning algorithm that partitions a dataset into a pre-determined number of non-overlapping subgroups by iteratively assigning each data point to the nearest cluster centre and then re-calculating the centroids based on the mean of the points in the cluster. The goal is to group data points such that those within the same cluster are as similar as possible, while those in different clusters are as different as possible, minimisig within-cluster sum of squared errors.
Procedure

Choose the number of clusters (\(k\))
Randomly assign initial cluster centres.
Assign each data point to the nearest centroid.
Update centroids to be the mean of their assigned points
Repeat 3 and 4 until assignments stop changing.



Optimal \(k\) is where adding more clusters doesn’t significantly improve how well the data is grouped. Strikes the balance between underfitting and and overfitting



Run k-means clustering for a range of \(k\) values (ex. 1-10)
For each \(k\), calculate the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS). This value is the measure of how close the data points in a cluster are to the cluster’s centroid. Lower WCSS imply tighter more cohesive clusters.
Plot \(k\) vs WCSS
Look for the ‘elbow’


As \(k\) increases, WCSS should decrease with the clusters getting tighter, but after a certain point, the improvement slows down. The ‘elbow’ is where the rate of decrease sharply changes. This is usually the optimal \(k\).

Goal Find countries with similar food security profiles.


Code
# Pivotting to Wider To have Numeric Values in Cells (split items)
food_wide <- food_security |> 
  filter(Year_End == 2020, Item %in% c("Average dietary energy supply adequacy (percent) (3-year average)", "Share of dietary energy supply derived from cereals, roots and tubers (percent) (3-year average)", "Gross domestic product per capita, PPP, (constant 2021 international $)", "Value of food imports in total merchandise exports (percent) (3-year average)","Per capita food supply variability (kcal/cap/day)", "Prevalence of obesity in the adult population (18 years and older) (percent)" )) |> 
  select(Area, Item, Value) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = Item, values_from = Value) |> 
  drop_na() 

# Standardising/Normalising Data 
food_scaled <- food_wide |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), scale))




Code
# iterate from 1 - 10 groups. Tot withins pulls the wss for the different groups.
wss_df <- tibble(k = 1:10) |> 
  mutate(wss = map_dbl(k,
                       ~kmeans(food_scaled  |> select(-Area),
                        centers = .x,
                        nstart = 25)$tot.withinss))
ggplot(wss_df, aes(k, wss)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Number of clusters K", y = "Total within-cluster sum of squares")















Important



Looks like we stop getting much improvement around \(k=5\) clusters. We will keep this as the number of clusters for our algorithm to fit.




Code
# Letting the library do all the work
k_best <- 5
kmeans_fit <- kmeans(food_scaled %>% select(-Area), centers = k_best, nstart = 25)

# Merging back to og set so we can plot
food_clustered <- broom::augment(kmeans_fit, food_scaled) |>  mutate(.cluster = as.factor(.cluster))

food_original_clustered <- food_wide |> 
  filter(Area %in% food_clustered$Area) |> 
  mutate(.cluster = food_clustered$.cluster)






Using the following inspiration.


Code
# Define discrete colors for each cluster
cluster_colors <- c("#469990", "#FA8072", "#B0C4DE", "#ffd8b1", "#dcbeff")

# Create empty plot
p <- plot_ly()

# separate trace for each cluster
for(i in 1:k_best) {
  cluster_data <- food_original_clustered |>  filter(.cluster == i)
  
p <- p |> 
    add_trace(
      data = cluster_data,
      type = 'splom',
      dimensions = list(
        list(label = 'Energy Adequacy (%)',
             values = ~`Average dietary energy supply adequacy (percent) (3-year average)`),
        list(label = 'Cereal Share (%)',
             values = ~`Share of dietary energy supply derived from cereals, roots and tubers (percent) (3-year average)`),
        list(label = 'GDP per Capita ($)',
             values = ~`Gross domestic product per capita, PPP, (constant 2021 international $)`),
        list(label = 'Food Imports (%)',
             values = ~`Value of food imports in total merchandise exports (percent) (3-year average)`),
        list(label = 'Supply Variability (kcal)',
             values = ~`Per capita food supply variability (kcal/cap/day)`),
        list(label = 'Obesity (%)',
             values = ~`Prevalence of obesity in the adult population (18 years and older) (percent)`)
      ),
      text = ~Area,
      name = paste("Cluster", i),
      marker = list(
        color = cluster_colors[i],
        size = 7,
        line = list(color = 'white', width = 0.5)
      ),
      showlegend = TRUE
    )
}

p <- p |> 
   layout(
    title = list(
      text = "Food Security K-Means Clustering (k=5)",
      font = list(size = 7)
    ),
    dragmode = 'select',
    hovermode = 'closest',
    # Make axes text smaller and rotated for readability
    xaxis = list(
      tickangle = 30,
      tickfont = list(size = 9),
      titlefont = list(size = 9)
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      tickfont = list(size = 9),
      titlefont = list(size = 9)
    ),
    # Margins and spacing
    margin = list(l = 70, r = 40, b = 70, t = 80),
    font = list(size = 7)
  )

p










You can double click on the cluster label on the right to isolate a trace, better visualise a cluster
You can hover on top of the points to see what area each value pertains to.
You can drag and select to highlight specific points of interest in any of these plots.
You can select and drag the axes labels for each individual plot to “scroll” to different areas of the plot.

title: K-Means Clustering Food Security
text:
About our data

Following the recommendation of experts gathered in the Committee on World Food Security (CFS) Round Table on hunger measurement, hosted at FAO headquarters in September 2011, an initial set of indicators aiming to capture various aspects of food insecurity is presented here. The choice of the indicators has been informed by expert judgment and the availability of data with sufficient coverage to enable comparisons across regions and over time.


food_security.csv








variable
class
description




Year_Start
integer
First year of this observation.


Year_End
integer
Final year of this observation.


Area
character
Country or region in which the observation took place.


Item
character
The specific indicator of food security.


Unit
character
Unit of the measurement. Here we load the prizes dataset from TidyTuesday and clean up missing degree entries. Then, we prefix degree names with letters (a–i) so we can later enforce a custom order - otherwise, ggsankey reorders them alphabetically.

title: UK Met Weather Data
text:
About this Data
This data was found on the TidyTuesday Repository
The UK Met Office is the United Kingdom’s national weather and climate service, providing forecasts, severe weather warnings, and climate science expertise. It helps people, businesses, and governments make informed decisions to stay safe and plan for the future. It was first established in 1854, making it one of the oldest weather services in the world.
Data has been scraped straight from the Met Office website and cleaned in a basic way. The few flags for “estimated” data and changing sunlight monitoring techniques have been removed for simplicity, but are available from the raw data. Also available is simple site metadata which includes the opening date and latitude and longitude of each station.

Monthly Historical information for 37 UK Meteorological Stations. Most go back to the early 1900s, but some go back as far as 1853. Station data files are updated on a rolling monthly basis, around 10 days after the end of the month. No allowances have been made for small site changes and developments in instrumentation.

title: On Par: Leveraging GPR for Perfect Golf, on Average
text: Full Report       Research Poster

title: On Par: Leveraging GPR for Perfect Golf, on Average
text:
A Brief Intro
During the summer of 2025, we developed a simulation-based framework to model optimal golf strategy through a statistical lens, recognising golf as a sequential decision-making problem under uncertainty. Our work combines player-specific shot data, course geometry, and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) to estimate the expected strokes to hole out (ESHO) and birdie probability surfaces across a golf hole.
By digitising course layouts and overlaying shot dispersion data from LPGA TrackMan records, we constructed spatially continuous GPR models that capture how club and aimpoint choices influence scoring outcomes. The model recursively works from the green backward - first fitting a 2D GPR to expected strokes on the putting surface, then extending the framework to evaluate approaches and tee shots, using simulated distributions to identify the optimal strategy for any point on the hole.
To accommodate different strategic objectives, we explored multiple loss functions: one minimizing expected strokes (for consistent performance) and another maximizing birdie odds (for high-stakes play). Together, these layers form a dynamic, player-adaptive decision system capable of evolving as new data are recorded.
This project demonstrates the potential of probabilistic modeling and spatial inference in sports analytics, offering a scalable foundation for real-time decision support in golf strategy - a step toward intelligent, data-driven gameplay.

Future Directions
I am currently in school and in the full swing of things, but I am working on finalising some drafts to publish our findings. The biggest limitation of our current framework is the lack of real shot-level data - datasets like the PGA Tour’s ShotLink system, which record every shot’s position and context, are not publicly accessible.
To address this, we designed a comprehensive data simulation pipeline that mirrors tournament-level patterns with surprising realism. We digitised course geometries in QGIS, and generated two-dimensional scoring distributions by interpolating Mark Broadie’s Strokes Gained tables. We introduced heteroscedastic noise to emulate real-world uncertainty and variance in shot outcomes, allowing our Gaussian Process Regression models to behave as if they were trained on noisy, heterogeneous field data. This in itself was a huge part of the project!
I am also working under the advising of Professor Vin De Silva during this year looking at potential topological interpretations of this research for my senior thesis! We don’t know exactly what we’re doing, but we have some time to figure it out!
Ultimately, this project represents both a proof of concept and a launchpad: a system already capable of personalized, data-driven strategy, and a framework ready to evolve into a publishable model as the data grows.

text:
This body of research is grounded in the study of gene expression timing, particularly in E. coli’s RpoS-dependent stress response. Understanding when a gene turns on (its onset time) is critical for interpreting cellular behaviour under stress.

title: Evaluating the Reliability of Sicegar for Timing Analysis of RpoS-Dependent Gene Expression
text:
A Brief Overview

Brief Context
This body of research is grounded in the study of gene expression timing, particularly in E. coli’s RpoS-dependent stress response. Understanding when a gene turns on (its onset time) is critical for interpreting cellular behaviour under stress.
To study this, Adams et al. (2023) used time-course RNA-seq data to observe gene expression trajectories and analysed them with the R package sicegar, a tool designed to model growth-like curves with sigmoidal or double-sigmoidal shapes. However, while sicegar has been widely used, its reliability in accurately identifying model type and estimating onset times had not been systematically validated. This project addresses that gap by building a simulation-based framework to test how well sicegar performs under controlled, known conditions.


Understanding sicegar
sicegar automatically fits data to both sigmoidal and double-sigmoidal models and chooses the better fit based on maximum likelihood estimation and AIC comparison.
It uses the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm to minimise squared residuals and normalises data to \([0,1]\) internally.
Its classification is intentionally conservative: when uncertain, it tends to label data as ambiguous rather than forcing a sigmoidal or double-sigmoidal classification.


The models

Sigmoidal model
Represents a single, monotonic increase in intensity until saturation: \[f(x) = h_0 + \frac{h_1-h_0}{1+e^{-a(x-t_1)}}\] where \(t_1\) corresponds to the inflection point and therefore to the onset time.


Double-sigmoidal model
Capture two distinct phases: an initial rise and a subsequent decline: \[f(x) = \frac{1}{h_1}\left(h_0 + \frac{h_1-h_0}{1+e^{-a_1(x-t_1)}}\right)\left(h_2 + \frac{h_1-h_2}{1+e^{a_2(x-t_2)}}\right)\] Here, the relationship between \(t_1\) and the actual onset time is not straightforward - \(t_1\) is not necessarily the true inflection point



Analytical and Computational Foundations
Before simulations, the project establishes theoretical ground truth for the inflection or onset time:

For the sigmoidal model, symbolic calculus confirmed that \(t_1\) indeed marks the inflection point.
For the double sigmoidal model, no closed-form solutions exists (trust me, we tried!). Analytical differentiation yields a highly complex expression. Therefore a numerical approach was developed for our research’s goals. We developed a computational pipeline that defined the true onset time for any onset time for any simulated double sigmoidal curve, providing a benchmark against which to test sicegar.



Simulation Design
Simulations generate synthetic gene expression data mimicking real experimental patterns with known ground truth.
Steps include:

Selecting model type (sigmoidal vs double-sigmoidal).
Choosing biologically realistic parameters.
Sampling at chosen intervals (we can ask, does sampling more often yield more accurate results?) and adding controlled noise (dispersion) and replicates to resemble experimental uncertainty.
Feeding the noisy data into sicegar’s fitAndCategorizefunction.

This approach mirrorss the logic of an experiment where both the “exam” (data) and “mark scheme” (true params) are known, allowing precise assessment of how close sicegar gets to the correct answers.


Brief Overview of Findings

Model identification
Simulations confirmed sicegar’s conservative classification behaviour:

It rarely misidentified models (sigmoid vs. double-sigmoid).
Instead, it tended to label uncertain cases as ambiguous, particularly at high noise levels.
Interestingly, some high-variability sigmoidal data were misclassified as double-sigmoidal, but not vice versa.



Onset Time Estimation - Sigmoidal Models
sicegar performed well under ideal (low-noise) conditions:

With zero dispersion, onset time detection was perfect (100% accuracy), though perhaps this is unsurprising.
As dispersion increased, the error increased systematically, typically underestimating onset times.
When recording time was too short (small x_lim), sicegar sometimes overestimated onset time instead.
Accuracy depended not just on noise but on how far the true onset was from the last observed timepoint - incomplete curves misled the model.



Onset Time Estimation - Double Sigmoidal Models
For double-sigmoids, the issue was more structural: - The first inflection point often did not coincide with sicegar’s reported \(t_1\). - Therefore, even with clean data, its interpretation of onset time was sometimes inaccurate by definition. - Nonetheless, sicegar’s model fititng was computationally efficient and stable - suggesting reliability in curve shape recognition, if not always in onset quantification.



Bootstrapping Bias Correction
After observing that both sigmoidal and double-sigmoidal models consistently underestimated onset time, we explored ways to quantify and correct this bias. Using the bootstrap method, we estimated the systematic deviation between sicegar’s onset time estimates and the true values. By resampling data and recalculating onset times across many iterations, we obtained an empirical distribution that revealed the average bias in estimation.
Because the data were sampled at discrete time points with limited replicates, a parametric bootstrap was developed. We first fitted a model using `sicegar, extracted its estimated parameters, and then generated new simulated datasets using those parameters. This allowed us to compute bootstrap-based bias estimates and adjust the original onset time accordingly. Across 500 datasets and 100 bootstraps per dataset, this correction systematically shifted the estimates closer to the true onset values.
Although we outlined a similar pipeline for the double-sigmoidal model, it remains computationally intensive to implement at scale due to nested simulations and the added complexity of identifying the correct inflection point.

title: Evaluating the Reliability of Sicegar for Timing Analysis of RpoS-Dependent Gene Expression
section: Curious About Where It Went Next?
text:
Curious About Where It Went Next?
The work presented in this paper is a small part of a larger research trajectory.
In the summer of 2024, immediately following the termination of our summer research period, Professor Jo Hardin presented our results at the Computational Genomics Summer Institute (CGSI) at UCLA, sharing both the methodological framework and the bootstrap correction we developed.
Throughout the 2024–2025 academic year, Mira Terdiman extended this work for their senior thesis under Hardin’s supervision. Their project focused on diagnosing estimation issues within the sicegar package - particularly those arising from corner cases in the sigmoidal and double-sigmoidal models, biases introduced by the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm, and the sensitivity of results to hyperparameter choices. Using simulations from known parameter values, they demonstrated that setting data-driven hyperparameters significantly improved the accuracy and reliability of fits, providing practical guidance for future users.
In the summer of 2025, three undergraduate collaborators continued this line of work with Professor Hardin by refining the underlying code and implementing Mira’s suggested changes directly within the package. Their fixes addressed several sources of bias and were formally submitted to the package authors - who integrated them into a new release. The team also co-authored a short software note in the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS), documenting these technical improvements and ensuring the methods could be reliably applied across diverse biological datasets.

title: Course Correction: Strategic Golf Powered by ML
text:
Final 1-Page Paper       5-min Presentation 

This 1-2 week project, Course Correction: Strategic Golf Powered by ML presents a personalized machine learning framework for optimizing golf club selection using player-specific TrackMan data and expected strokes to hole out (ESHO) based on lie and distance. By implementing Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) models for different lies (green, fairway, rough, sand), the framework simulates outcomes for various clubs and aimpoints, recommending strategies that minimise expected strokes under both neutral and goal-oriented loss functions. Using data from Pomona-Pitzer tournament rounds and a D3 golfer’s TrackMan shots, the model accounts for dispersion patterns and identifies optimal club-aimpoint combinations for scenarios such as birdie or par targets.
This was a first attempt or look at what would become my greater summer project Gaussian Process Regression for Golf.

title: Golf’s Golden Ratio – A Statistical Analysis of Tempo & Driving Distance
text:
Final Paper 

This small project, Golf’s Golden Ratio – A Statistical Analysis of Tempo & Driving Distance, investigates the relationship between backswing duration and average driving distance for professional female golfers on the LPGA Tour. Using a sample of 40 players, the study collected average driving distances from official LPGA statistics and measured backswing times from slowed-down video footage, while also accounting for player height. Through multiple linear regression analysis, the results indicate a statistically significant negative correlation between backswing duration and driving distance- faster backswings are associated with longer drives—while height does not have a meaningful effect. The study suggests that backswing tempo is a more predictive factor of driving performance than physical stature and highlights potential implications for coaching and performance optimisation in golf.

title: Oh My Gas! A Time Series Analysis of California Gas Prices
text:
Paper 

This project, Oh My Gas! A Time Series Analysis of California Gas Prices, examines weekly retail prices of California’s regular reformulated gasoline from 1995 to 2024 using SARIMA modeling to understand trends and forecast future prices. After log-transforming and differencing the data to achieve stationarity, autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation analyses suggested both short-term (weekly and monthly) and seasonal (yearly) dependencies. The final \(SARIMA(4,1,0)×(1,0,1)_{52}\) model captures these dynamics, showing that the most recent week, the preceding month, and the same week in prior years are the strongest predictors of current prices. While the model demonstrates predictive capability, it also highlights the high volatility of California gas prices, emphasizing the difficulty of precise forecasting and the inherent uncertainty in the market.

title: Putting Myths to Rest: Spectral Analysis of PGA Tour Metrics
text:
Paper 

This project, Putting Myths to Rest: Spectral Analysis of PGA Tour Metrics, investigates whether elite PGA Tour golfers exhibit “streakiness” in their putting performance using spectral domain analysis. Focusing on Strokes Gained Putting averages from 2015–2022 for top-ranked players, the analysis of autocorrelation functions, periodograms, and cumulative periodograms indicates that variations in putting performance resemble white noise, with little to no serial correlation or cyclical patterns. These results dispel the popular belief in predictable “hot” streaks, suggesting that putting success in professional golf is largely random and independent across tournaments.

title: Lead concentration in Flint water samples in 2015
text:
In 2014, Flint, Michigan switched its water source to the Flint River to save money. Almost immediately, residents complained about discoloured, foul-smelling water. By 2015, independent researchers and concerned residents began testing for lead contamination. Under the federal Lead and Copper Rule, if the 90th percentile of water samples exceeds 15 parts per billion (ppb), the water system must take corrective action. When initial tests showed Flint’s 90th percentile at a dangerous level well above this threshold, Michigan Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) officials faced a crisis: not of public health, but of accountability. Their solution? Remove the highest-reading samples from the dataset on questionable technical grounds, including dismissing a sample of 104 ppb from activist Lee-Anne Walters’ home because she had requested a faucet filter weeks earlier. This wasn’t just poor judgment, it was deliberate data manipulation, a textbook case of cherry-picking results to reach a predetermined conclusion. By systematically excluding the worst contamination readings, officials manufactured a false sense of safety while residents, including thousands of children, continued drinking poisoned water. What follows is the visual story of how changing the data changed the outcome.






This visualisation was built in D3.js. You can find the code for this visualisation in the following repository.

title: Lead concentration in Flint water samples in 2015
text:
What Happened?
The removal of high-lead samples from MDEQ’s official data raised serious concerns about data manipulation. By excluding samples with lead levels above the EPA action level, the 90th percentile was artificially lowered from 18 ppb to 11.4 ppb, making the water appear safer than it actually was.
This sparked a citizen science effort led by Virginia Tech researchers to independently test Flint’s water, ultimately exposing the crisis.

log_scale + nonlog_scale











This dual visualisation explores the financial distribution of Brazilian companies by the role of their owners, using the national colors to segment the data into key quantiles (from the 25th to the 99th percentile). The Log Scale plot on the left provides a “balanced” view; by compressing the massive range of capital values, it reveals that nearly every owner role follows a similar internal hierarchy where the top 1% (q99) holds vastly more capital than the median (q50). This view allows us to learn about the roles with lower overall capital, such as Liquidators or Legal Representatives, which would otherwise be invisible.
Conversely, the Regular Scale plot on the right exposes the “absolute” economic reality of wealth concentration in Brazil. When viewed linearly, the logarithmic balancing effect vanishes, replaced by sharp spikes: most notably for Directors and President/Chairs. This comparison demonstrates that while the internal distribution of capital is skewed across all roles, the total volume of capital is dominated by a select few elite positions.

text: To visualise how the emotional tone of the Sherlock Holmes series evolved, we first had to place each story in time. The raw text data provided the narratives, but lacked publication metadata. We then standardised the book titles (converting them to lowercase and removing punctuation) to create a common key, allowing us to successfully join the publication years to the main text dataset.

title: The Flint Water Crisis: A Story of Data Manipulation
text:
When Officials Cooked the Books
In 2014, Flint, Michigan switched its water source to the Flint River to save money. Almost immediately, residents complained about discolored, foul-smelling water. By 2015, independent researchers and concerned residents began testing for lead contamination. Under the federal Lead and Copper Rule, if the 90th percentile of water samples exceeds 15 parts per billion (ppb), the water system must take corrective action. When initial tests showed Flint’s 90th percentile at a dangerous level well above this threshold, Michigan Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) officials faced a crisis—not of public health, but of accountability. Their solution? Remove the highest-reading samples from the dataset on questionable technical grounds, including dismissing a sample of 104 ppb from activist Lee-Anne Walters’ home because she had requested a faucet filter weeks earlier. This wasn’t just poor judgment—it was deliberate data manipulation, a textbook case of cherry-picking results to reach a predetermined conclusion. By systematically excluding the worst contamination readings, officials manufactured a false sense of safety while residents, including thousands of children, continued drinking poisoned water. What follows is the visual story of how changing the data changed the outcome.








THE CRISIS BEGINS
In 2015, residents of Flint reported foul-smelling, discolored water. Officials insisted it was safe. Residents began testing it themselves.




THE SAMPLES
Hundreds of bottles flooded in. Each droplet here represents one home’s water sample. Watch the distribution build.




THE FEDERAL LIMIT
The EPA sets the Action Level at 15 ppb. If the 90th percentile of samples exceeds this line, the city must take immediate action.




A CLEAR VIOLATION
The initial calculation was damning. The 90th percentile was well into the Danger Zone. Flint officials faced a crisis.




THE MANIPULATION
MDEQ officials needed the number to be lower. They invalidated high-lead samples on technicalities, like Lee-Anne Walters’ 104 ppb sample (excluded for a ‘filter’).




AN ERASURE PROBLEM
By discarding the worst offenders, the dataset was fundamentally altered. Watch the removed samples vanish.




MANUFACTURED SAFETY
With the data manipulated, the 90th percentile slid just barely below the line. The water was declared ‘Safe’.

title: Brazilian Companies
text:
Code
quantile_data <- companies |> # removing intervenor
  filter(owner_qualification != "Intervenor / Court-appointed Administrator") |> 
  mutate(owner_qualification = case_match( # shortening names so that they are not cut in the plot
    owner_qualification,
    "Managing Partner / Partner-Administrator" ~ "Managing Partner",
    "Beneficial Owner (individual) resident or domiciled in Brazil" ~ "Resident Owner",
    "Administrator / Manager" ~ "Manager",
    "Entrepreneur / Business Owner" ~ "Entrepreneur",
    "President / Chair" ~ "President/Chair",
    "Director / Officer" ~ "Director",
    "Ostensible Partner (Managing partner in a silent partnership)" ~ "Silent Partner",
    "Sole Owner of an Individual Real Estate Company" ~ "Real Estate Owner",
    "Judicial Administrator (Court-appointed)" ~ "Court Admin",
    "Attorney-in-fact / Legal Representative (Power of Attorney)" ~ "Legal Rep",
    "Executor / Estate Administrator" ~ "Estate Admin",
    .default = owner_qualification # Keeps Liquidator as is
  )) |> 
  # wrap text - don't stretch the plot
  mutate(owner_qualification = stringr::str_wrap(owner_qualification, width = 12)) |> 
  group_by(owner_qualification) |> 
  summarise(q25 = quantile(capital_stock, p = 0.25), # computing percentiles for the plot
            q50 = quantile(capital_stock, p = 0.5),
            q75 = quantile(capital_stock, p = 0.75),
            q95 = quantile(capital_stock, p = 0.95),
            q99 = quantile(capital_stock, p = 0.99)) |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = q25:q99, names_to = "percentile", values_to = "quantile")


The raw CNPJ (Cadastro Nacional da Pessoa Jurídica) dataset contains highly detailed legal terminology that requires refinement before it can be visualised or understood. I performed several key transformations to prepare the data for the comparative analysis:

I removed the category Intervenor / Court-appointed Administrator to focus the analysis on standard business ownership and management roles rather than temporary legal interventions.
I renamed long, technical legal titles into concise equivalents to prevent the text from running off the screen and ensuring the polar plot remains readable.
Even after shortening, some labels remained long. I applied stringr::str_wrap with a width of 12 characters to ensure that the labels would sit neatly around the circular axis without overlapping or forcing the plot to shrink.
Because capital stock in Brazil is highly skewed, a simple mean would be misleading. Instead, I computed five specific percentiles: \(Q_{25}, Q_{50}, Q_{75}, Q_{95}, Q_{99}\).
Finally, I used pivot_longer to move the calculated quantiles into a long format so that we could stack the data in the plot.



Code
library(patchwork)
# brazil theme palette
brazil_green <- "#009739"
flag_palette <- c("#FFDF00", "#FFEC70", "#4DA6FF", "#002776", "#01153E")

log_scale <- quantile_data |> 
  mutate(percentile = forcats::fct_rev(percentile)) |>  #factor for stacks
  ggplot(aes(x = owner_qualification, y = quantile)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = percentile), stat = "identity", 
           width = 1, color = brazil_green, linewidth = 0.2) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = flag_palette) +
  scale_y_log10(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) + #nice scale
  coord_polar() + 
  labs(
    title = "CAPITAL STOCK BY OWNER ROLE\nLog Scale",
    subtitle = "Financial distribution across Brazilian legal entities",
    caption = "Data: TidyTuesday January 2026 | Federica & Friends"
  ) +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = brazil_green, colour = brazil_green),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = brazil_green, colour = brazil_green),
    text = element_text(family = "montserrat", color = "#FFDF00"), # contrasting colour
    # nice settings for titles
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, margin = margin(t = 20), hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "white", margin = margin(b = 10), hjust = 0.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8, margin = margin(t = 10), hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(color = "white", size = 9, face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(5, 5, 5, 5), 
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = brazil_green, colour = "NA"),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = brazil_green, colour = "white")
  )

nonlog_scale <- quantile_data |> 
  mutate(percentile = forcats::fct_rev(percentile)) |>  #factor for stacks
  ggplot(aes(x = owner_qualification, y = quantile)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = percentile), stat = "identity", 
           width = 1, color = brazil_green, linewidth = 0.2) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = flag_palette) +
  coord_polar() + 
  labs(
    title = "CAPITAL STOCK BY OWNER ROLE\nRegular Scale",
    subtitle = "Financial distribution across Brazilian legal entities",
    caption = "Data: TidyTuesday January 2026 | Federica & Friends"
  ) +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = brazil_green, colour = brazil_green),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = brazil_green, colour = brazil_green),
    text = element_text(family = "montserrat", color = "#FFDF00"), # contrasting colour
    # nice settings for titles
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, margin = margin(t = 20), hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "white", margin = margin(b = 10), hjust = 0.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8, margin = margin(t = 10), hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(color = "white", size = 9, face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(5, 5, 5, 5), 
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = brazil_green, colour = "NA"),
    legend.key = element_rect(fill = brazil_green, colour = "white")
  )

log_scale + nonlog_scale

title: Brazilian Companies
text:
Comparison of Capital Stock Scaling
This dual visualisation explores the financial distribution of Brazilian companies by the role of their owners, using the national colors to segment the data into key quantiles (from the 25th to the 99th percentile). The Log Scale plot on the left provides a “balanced” view; by compressing the massive range of capital values, it reveals that nearly every owner role follows a similar internal hierarchy where the top 1% (q99) holds vastly more capital than the median (q50). This view allows us to learn about the roles with lower overall capital, such as Liquidators or Legal Representatives, which would otherwise be invisible.
Conversely, the Regular Scale plot on the right exposes the “absolute” economic reality of wealth concentration in Brazil. When viewed linearly, the logarithmic balancing effect vanishes, replaced by sharp spikes: most notably for Directors and President/Chairs. This comparison demonstrates that while the internal distribution of capital is skewed across all roles, the total volume of capital is dominated by a select few elite positions.

log_scale + nonlog_scale











This dual visualisation explores the financial distribution of Brazilian companies by the role of their owners, using the national colors to segment the data into key quantiles (from the 25th to the 99th percentile). The Log Scale plot on the left provides a “balanced” view; by compressing the massive range of capital values, it reveals that nearly every owner role follows a similar internal hierarchy where the top 1% (q99) holds vastly more capital than the median (q50). This view allows us to learn about the roles with lower overall capital, such as Liquidators or Legal Representatives, which would otherwise be invisible.
Conversely, the Regular Scale plot on the right exposes the “absolute” economic reality of wealth concentration in Brazil. When viewed linearly, the logarithmic balancing effect vanishes, replaced by sharp spikes: most notably for Directors and President/Chairs. This comparison demonstrates that while the internal distribution of capital is skewed across all roles, the total volume of capital is dominated by a select few elite positions.

title: Tidy Tuesday - Pi Digits
text:
This week’s dataset is just the first million digits of \(\pi\). Rather than doing anything mathematical with them, the fun question is: does your birthday show up in \(\pi\)?
Every birthday can be written as a 4-digit string (MMDD, e.g. 0324 for 24 March). Since \(\pi\)’s digits are believed to be normal (every digit sequence appears about as often as you’d expect by chance), we’d expect essentially every possible 4-digit MMDD string to turn up somewhere in the first million digits - some more often than others just by luck.
So the plan is:

Build a table of all 366 calendar dates (including 29 Feb) as MMDD strings.
Slide a 4-digit window along the digits of \(\pi\) and record every 4-digit sequence that appears, and where.
Join the two on the MMDD string, so each calendar date picks up every position in \(\pi\) where its birthday string occurs.
Plot how many times each date’s birthday shows up.

# Colour palette

  filter(regime == "Realistic") %>%
  select(pattern, cache_size, lru_miss_rate, rma_miss_rate) %>%
  pivot_longer(

    names_to  = "algorithm",
    values_to = "miss_rate"
  ) %>%

    algorithm  = recode(algorithm, lru_miss_rate = "LRU", rma_miss_rate = "RMA"),

# ============================================================
# 1. RAW TEXT DATA
# ============================================================
pdf_text_data <- "
Statistics Probability Data Science Teaching Assistant

end-to-end data generation modeling pipeline Python R

generated noisy samples empirical ShotLink baselines
heuristic difficulty multipliers simulate realistic putting heteroscedasticity

Gaussian Process Regression GPR continuous non-parametric latent scoring surfaces
Expected Strokes Hole Out binary Birdie Probabilities
Python GPyTorch large-scale Monte Carlo simulations
stochastic shot outcomes bivariate Gaussian distributions
linear transformations rotation matrices
dispersion patterns variable aimpoints
Bellman Principle Optimality recursive optimization

Residence Advisor supervisory residential community

model selection R code Sicegar ImpulseDE2 DESeq2

"

missing_data <- "
Magna Cum Laude 3.978 GPA
Captain Varsity Women Golf Association Women Mathematics AWM Claremont

Academic Honours Latin Honours
Magna Cum Laude

Senior Thesis Distinction Math Moral Compromise Beyond Arrow Impossibility

Gaussian Process Regression optimise strategic decision-making

Bernard Charnwut Chan Leadership Service Award
Sheri Sangji Memorial Award

Captain Varsity Women Golf Team
Conference Champions team titles
NCAA National appearances Individual National Titles
All-Conference All-Region individual wins
"

full_text <- paste(pdf_text_data, missing_data, sep = " ")


# ============================================================
# 2. TEXT CLEANING
# ============================================================
corpus <- Corpus(VectorSource(full_text)) |>
  tm_map(content_transformer(tolower)) |>
  tm_map(removePunctuation) |>
  tm_map(removeNumbers)

ignore_words <- c(
  stopwords("english"),
  # Locations / dates
  "page", "claremont", "madrid", "california", "united", "states", "spain",
  "january", "february", "march", "april", "may", "june", "july", "august",
  "september", "october", "november", "december", "months", "years", "semesters",
  # Contact noise
  "gmailcom", "wwwlinkedincominfedericadomecqlacroze", "linkedin",
  # Filler
  "also", "using", "used", "use", "well", "across", "within", "including",
  "served", "served", "focused", "designed", "executed", "based", "etc"
)

corpus <- tm_map(corpus, removeWords, ignore_words)

Warning in tm_map.SimpleCorpus(corpus, removeWords, ignore_words):
transformation drops documents

dtm   <- TermDocumentMatrix(corpus)
mat   <- as.matrix(dtm)
words <- sort(rowSums(mat), decreasing = TRUE)
df    <- data.frame(word = names(words), freq = words, row.names = NULL)

# Remove single-character tokens
df <- df |> filter(nchar(as.character(word)) > 1)

# ---- Strategic frequency boosting ----
core_anchors <- c(
  "statistics", "mathematics", "golf", "regression", "gaussian",
  "probability", "computing", "science", "research", "python",
  "modeling", "optimization", "data", "analysis"
)
df <- df |>
  mutate(freq = ifelse(word %in% core_anchors, freq * 4, freq))

# Keep a dense copy for shape-filling (repeat so tails have enough words)
df_dense <- bind_rows(df, df, df, df) |>
  slice_max(freq, n = 400)   # cap at 400 for speed


# ============================================================
# 3. CUSTOM FONT  (Fraunces — matches your website headings)
# ============================================================
# showtext pulls from Google Fonts at render time — no local install needed
font_add_google("Fraunces", "fraunces")   # serif, distinctive
font_add_google("Space Grotesk", "space") # your site sans-serif (fallback labels)
showtext_auto()   # tell ggplot2 to use showtext for text rendering


# ============================================================
# 4A. GENERATE THE BELL-CURVE MASK IMAGE
# ============================================================
# CRITICAL: Save the mask SQUARE (same pixel width & height).
# ggwordcloud reads the mask as a raw pixel matrix — if the image is
# wide and short, the "curve" becomes a flat ellipse in pixel-space.
# We generate a square mask and let ggsave handle the final banner crop.

x <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 2000)
y <- dnorm(x)
bell_data <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

bell_mask_plot <- ggplot(bell_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_area(fill = "black") +
  # Add white padding above the curve so the bell sits in the lower half
  # of a square — this gives the words vertical room to stack up the sides
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.8), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0.02, 0.02)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin      = margin(0, 0, 0, 0)
  )

# SQUARE — same width and height in inches, high DPI for crisp edges
ggsave("bell_curve_mask.png", plot = bell_mask_plot,
       width = 8, height = 8, dpi = 300, bg = "white")


# ============================================================
# 4B. BELL-CURVE WORD CLOUD  (LinkedIn Banner proportions)
# ============================================================
mask_img    <- readPNG("bell_curve_mask.png")
# Safely handle RGB or RGBA
mask_matrix <- if (length(dim(mask_img)) == 3) mask_img[,,1] < 0.5 else mask_img < 0.5

set.seed(42)
bell_cloud <- ggplot(
  df_dense,
  aes(label = word,
      size  = freq,
      color = factor(sample(1:2, nrow(df_dense), replace = TRUE)),
      family = "fraunces")          # <-- Fraunces font
) +
  geom_text_wordcloud(
    mask       = mask_matrix,
    rm_outside = TRUE,
    grid_size  = 1,
    max_steps  = 500,
    seed       = 42
  ) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#9E7E38", "#111111")) +  # WFU gold + black
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin      = margin(2, 2, 2, 2, "mm")
  )

img <- image_read("bell_curve_wordcloud_square.png")
# Crop a wide strip from the vertical center where the bell sits
info   <- image_info(img)
crop_h <- as.integer(info$width / 4)          # 4:1 aspect ratio height
crop_y <- as.integer((info$height - crop_h) * 0.55)  # slightly below center
banner <- image_crop(img, geometry_area(info$width, crop_h, 0, crop_y))
image_write(banner, "bell_curve_wordcloud_banner.png")


# ============================================================
# 5.  WFU LOGO WORD CLOUD
# ============================================================
# IMPORTANT — your logo PNG must be:
#   • Black pixels where you want words to appear
#   • White background everywhere else
#   • Saved as ./WakeForestImage.png  (or change the path below)
#
# If your logo is on a transparent/white background with a dark logo,
# it will work as-is.  If the logo is LIGHT on DARK, invert it in any
# image editor (or run the inversion chunk below first).

logo_path <- "./WakeForestImage.png"

if (file.exists(logo_path)) {

  logo_img    <- readPNG(logo_path)
  # Handle RGB, RGBA, or grayscale
  if (length(dim(logo_img)) == 3 && dim(logo_img)[3] >= 3) {
    # Use luminance: dark pixels (logo) become TRUE
    luminance   <- 0.299 * logo_img[,,1] + 0.587 * logo_img[,,2] + 0.114 * logo_img[,,3]
    logo_matrix <- luminance < 0.5
  } else if (length(dim(logo_img)) == 3) {
    logo_matrix <- logo_img[,,1] < 0.5
  } else {
    logo_matrix <- logo_img < 0.5
  }

  set.seed(42)
  wfu_cloud <- ggplot(
    df_dense,
    aes(label = word,
        size  = freq,
        color = factor(sample(1:2, nrow(df_dense), replace = TRUE)),
        family = "fraunces")
  ) +
    geom_text_wordcloud(
      mask       = logo_matrix,
      rm_outside = TRUE,
      grid_size  = 1,
      max_steps  = 500,
      seed       = 42
    ) +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 7) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("#9E7E38", "#111111")) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
      plot.margin      = margin(2, 2, 2, 2, "mm")
    )

  wfu_cloud

  ggsave("wfu_logo_wordcloud_banner.png",
         plot   = wfu_cloud,
         width  = 15.84, height = 3.96,
         dpi    = 300, bg = "white")

} else {
  message("WakeForestImage.png not found — skipping logo cloud.")
  message("Place your WFU logo PNG in the same folder as this .qmd file.")
}

Other Work
Approximately every week for the last two years, I have participated in tidytuesday, which is a weekly social data project with the opportunity to wrangle analyse and visualise new datasets everyweek. As of the creation of this website, I will start to upload my work here.

A little about me
When I’m not working on a problem set or a paper, I’m usually outside — golfing, doing something creative, or, lately, learning pickleball. I like trying new sports and staying active. 
I am currently part of the Pomona-Pitzer’s Varsity Women’s Golf team — I served as 2-year Team Captain, made 3 NCAA National appearances, and won 2 individual national titles, hence this colourful theme!










On the course with Pomona-Pitzer Golf







A favourite spot in Claremont







Tech & tools
Tools I feel comfortable with include R, Python, Java, JavaScript, and HTML / SCSS. I use tidyverse-style workflows for data wrangling and visualisation, and I’ve worked with HPC for large simulations, as well as GPyTorch for Gaussian Process modeling.

At this moment in time, I’m wrapping up my time at Pomona and gearing up to start my M.S. in Statistics at Wake Forest University this fall, while continuing to seek data science / analytics opportunities that combine problem-solving, creativity, and impact — where I can keep learning and contribute to meaningful projects. If that sounds like a fit, let’s connect! ✨

title: On Arrow’s Impossibility
text:
with Dr Ami Radunskaya



Can a group of people ever aggregate their preferences into a single, fair decision? This page holds my senior thesis in Mathematics, The Math of Moral Compromise: Beyond Arrow’s Impossibility, which traces the history of voting theory, proves Arrow’s Impossibility Theorem in full, and reframes it through a topological lens using ultrafilters.

title: On Par Golf 2026: Extending the Framework
text:
Pasatiempo GC, CA



This page tracks the next chapter of my Golf On Par Paper, the Gaussian Process Regression framework for golf strategy I built in Summer ’25. Since December 2025, I’ve been extending it into a full manuscript for peer-reviewed publication with Professor Jo Hardin — formalising the multi-fidelity model that fuses simulated and real-outcome data, running convergence and sensitivity analyses, and pushing the framework closer to something that could genuinely inform how a player approaches a hole.
This work is still in progress. The manuscript isn’t finished or submitted yet, so there’s no paper to share here just yet. In the meantime, you can read about where the project started on the Summer ’25 project page. Or check out the slides for my eCOTS 2026 presentation.

title: Goodbye Golf!
text:
This story is under construction! Coming Soon!






Caption 1







Caption 2







Caption 3







Caption 4





At age of six, I was fortunate enough to travel from Madrid to Florida where my parents and I were to “help” my grandmother, Mercedes Lacroze, move back to Argentina. I didn’t know it then, but that coastal Florida stopover would hold my first introduction to the game of golf.
While I have a strong of images in my head that allow me to recall all the circumstances, the name of my very first coach is lost to time. Shelly, Shane, Shaina, or Sharlene– I am confident that her name started with “S-H”. Looking back now as someone who has spent time teaching on the driving range, what seemed strange to a six-year-old makes brilliant sense today. The genius she was, Shelly decided to save me from the frustration of whiffing of whiffing every shot, in our first lesson. Instead, she tasked me with snapping an entire box of wooden tees stuck in the turf. Once I had proven exceptionally skilled at tee-destruction, she granted me my official “ball license.” The final rule, repeated like a mantra down the line: hold your finish until the ball comes to a complete stop.
Golf remained a sporadic hobby for years. Back in Madrid, Saturday lessons at the local public course felt tedious and dull. It was only during visits with my grandmother—whom we called Mem—that the game took on real meaning.
To understand why, you first have to understand Mem. She was, quite simply, an icon.
She originally took up golf to shed pregnancy weight and share an activity with my grandfather, but the game quickly became an obsession. She would leave her newborn in the clubhouse, play nine holes, come back to nurse, and head right back out for nine more. Before long, she left my grandfather in the dust—literally driving him to quit the game because he couldn’t match her pace. Mem went on to hit a scratch handicap in the era of wooden-headed clubs, capturing the Argentine National Championship and the Copa Los Andes along the way.
Then, in her late 20s, she walked away cold.
On the eve of the final round of a major tournament—one she had never won, holding a three-stroke lead over a rival she’d never beaten—she was practicing her putting at home when my grandfather suffered a heart attack. Rushing to the hospital, Mem realized with a shock that part of her mind was still fixated on her morning tee time. Terrified by that shift in priorities, she never returned to the locker room to pick up her clubs. My grandfather was later diagnosed with cancer and given a grim prognosis, but Mem brought him to the U.S. for treatment, extending his life by ten full years. She only touched a club again decades later, when her youngest son wanted to learn the game for business.

library(tidyverse)
library(cartogram)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

world_castles <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-09-01/world_castles.csv')
world_map <- map_data("world")

# For nicer fonts
font_add_google("Space Grotesk", "space_grotesk")
font_add_google("Inter", "inter")
showtext_auto()
showtext_opts(dpi = 300)

bgy <- "#f6ecda"  
titles <-  "#141414"
other_text <- "#4c7a5a"
continent_fill <-  "#1f1f1fea"
continent_outline <- "#a1a1a1"
opac <- 0.85

# colours for hexbins
castle_fill_scale <- scale_fill_gradientn(
  colours = c("#18261c", "#2f4f38", "#4c7a5a", "#85b090", "#b8d4be"),
  name   = "# of castles",
  na.value = "transparent"
)

fame_fill_scale <- scale_fill_gradientn(
  colours = c("#2b1a2e", "#6b2d3c", "#a8452f", "#d97a2b", "#f2b134", "#f7dfa0"),
  name   = "fame weight",
  na.value = "transparent"
)
  
base_map_theme <- theme_void(base_family = "space_grotesk") +
  theme(
    plot.background   = element_rect(fill = bgy, colour = NA),
    panel.background  = element_rect(fill = bgy, colour = NA),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(colour =titles, size = 14, face = "bold",
                              hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 4)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = other_text, size = 11,
                                 hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    legend.position  = "bottom",
    legend.title     = element_text(colour = other_text, size = 9),
    legend.text      = element_text(colour = other_text, size = 8),
    strip.text       = element_text(colour = other_text, face = "bold", size = 10),
    plot.margin      = margin(4, 4, 4, 4)
  )

title: Tidy Tuesday - World Castles, Fortresses and Palaces
text:
About this Data
This data comes from Tidy Tuesday
This week we’re exploring the Castlemap dataset of 5,793 castles, fortresses, palaces and ruins in 138 countries. The data comes from Wikidata, and every landmark has verified coordinates, a Wikipedia article and a photo on Wikimedia Commons. Each also has a fame rank, based on how many languages have an article on it and how often that article is read. The Great Wall of China is first.

Which countries have the most castles?
Are palaces newer than fortresses?
Which landmarks have articles in many languages but few readers?

Thank you to Georgios Karamanis for curating this week’s dataset.

title: Tidy Tuesday - World Castles, Fortresses and Palaces
text:
Data Dictionary

world_castles.csv








variable
class
description




qid
character
Wikidata item ID, e.g. Q1067425.


name
character
Landmark name, in English where available, e.g. Neuschwanstein Castle.


category
character
Type of landmark: castle, fortress, palace or ruin.


country
character
Country the landmark is in, e.g. France. The UK constituent countries are listed separately, e.g. Scotland.


iso
character
ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code, e.g. FR. The UK constituent countries use ISO 3166-2 subdivision codes, e.g. GB-SCT.


lat
double
Latitude in WGS84 decimal degrees, e.g. 48.80472.


lon
double
Longitude in WGS84 decimal degrees, e.g. 2.12028.


year
double
Founding year, e.g. 1661. Negative for BC dates, e.g. -3000.


year_approx
double
Whether the founding year is an estimate, 1, or a documented date, 0.


century
character
Century the founding year falls in, e.g. 17th century or 30th century BC.


wikipedia
character
URL of the Wikipedia article, e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Versailles.


image
character
URL of a Wikimedia Commons photo, e.g. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Alhambra%20detail.jpg?width=1280.


sitelinks
double
Number of Wikipedia language editions with an article on the landmark, e.g. 95.


pageviews
double
Wikipedia pageviews over the trailing 365 days, e.g. 756430.


fame_rank
double
Global fame rank, blending sitelinks and pageviews, where 1 is the most famous.

title: Tidy Tuesday - World Castles, Fortresses and Palaces
text:
What are hexbins?
Our choice of data visualisations are hexbins which are a way to represent dense 2d data sets by binning individual data points into hexagonal shapes with different hues. The colour of the hexagonal shapes denotes the number of points (in this case number of castles), fall within its area.
The benefits of hexbins include:

They prevent overplotting by summarising the density of an area
They reduce visual bias, they connect smoothly and therefore have less directional bias than other shapes (say if we plotted squares) since the distance to its neighbours is equal.
They work well with maps given that they can replace irregular geographic regions :D

title: Tidy Tuesday - World Castles, Fortresses and Palaces
text:
Castles around the World

Looking at the Distribution of Castles All Around the World
Nothing too crazy here. We use geom_hex to plot the hexbins on a world map. We plot a world map below in order to help the viewer with their contextual awareness.


Code
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = continent_fill, colour = NA, alpha = opac) +  # outline below
  geom_hex(data = world_castles, aes(x = lon, y = lat), bins = 100, alpha = 1) + # check different bins
  geom_polygon(data = world_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = NA, colour = continent_outline, size = 0.08) +  # outline above
  castle_fill_scale +
  coord_fixed(1.3, expand = FALSE) +
  base_map_theme +
  labs(title = "Castles All Around the World",
      subtitle = "Lighter hexagons denote a higher number of castles!")









Unsuprisingly, majority of the indexed castles seem to be in Europe, but we quite genuinely can find castles everywhere around the world!


Are there differences between these distribution depending on the castle type?
Since our dataset discretises between castles, fortresses, palaces and ruins, we might care to observe these differences.

title: Tidy Tuesday - World Castles, Fortresses and Palaces
text:
What About Popularity?
So far every castle has counted for exactly one hexagon’s worth of colour, regardless of whether it’s the Great Wall of China or a deserted castle nobody has heard of. But the dataset gives us fame_rank (a blend of Wikipedia sitelinks and pageviews, where 1 is the most famous landmark on Earth).

Turning fame into weight
fame_rank is a rank, so a smaller number means more famous. To make popular castles pull harder on the map we flip it into a “fame weight”: the top-ranked castle gets the biggest weight, and the weight shrinks as we move down the ranking. Then we uncount() by that weight so a very famous castle contributes many points to the hexbin instead of just one.


Code
n_castles <- max(world_castles$fame_rank, na.rm = TRUE)

world_castles_pop <- world_castles |>
  filter(!is.na(fame_rank)) |>
  mutate(fame_weight = round((n_castles - fame_rank + 1) / n_castles * 40) + 1) |>
  uncount(fame_weight)


Every castle still shows up at least once, but the famous ones now count for up to 40, so the hexbins lean towards where the well-known castles are rather the sheer count of castles.


The popularity-weighted world


Code
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = continent_fill, colour = NA, alpha = opac) +  # outline below
  geom_hex(data = world_castles_pop, aes(x = lon, y = lat), bins = 200, alpha = 1) +
  geom_polygon(data = world_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = NA, colour = continent_outline, size = 0.08) +  # outline above
  fame_fill_scale +
  coord_fixed(1.3, expand = FALSE) +
  base_map_theme +
  labs(title = "The World's Castles, Weighted by Fame",
       subtitle = "Each castle counts more the more famous it is (fame_rank)")









Europe still dominates, but theres definitely a bright hotspot in East Asia around the Great Wall and the Chinese and Japanese palace-cities.


Let’s look at Asia and Europe
Let’s look at them both simultaneously!


Code
asia_map <- ne_countries(continent = "Asia", scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")

europe_pop <- world_castles_pop |> filter(continent == "Europe")

title: Tidy Tuesday - Pi Digits
text:
This week’s dataset is just the first million digits of \(\pi\). Rather than doing anything mathematical with them, the fun question is: does your birthday show up in \(\pi\)?
Every birthday can be written as a 4-digit string (MMDD, e.g. 0324 for 24 March). Since \(\pi\)’s digits are believed to be normal (every digit sequence appears about as often as you’d expect by chance), we’d expect essentially every possible 4-digit MMDD string to turn up somewhere in the first million digits - some more often than others just by luck.
So the plan is:

Build a table of all 366 calendar dates (including 29 Feb) as MMDD strings.
Slide a 4-digit window along the digits of \(\pi\) and record every 4-digit sequence that appears, and where.
Join the two on the MMDD string, so each calendar date picks up every position in \(\pi\) where its birthday string occurs.
Plot how many times each date’s birthday shows up.



Code
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
pi_digits <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-03-24/pi_digits.csv')


As a sanity check, let’s confirm we can actually find a known chunk of \(\pi\) (3.14159…26535…) in the data before completing the rest of our mission.


Code
pi_digits |>
  filter(digit == 0,
         lead(digit) == 1,
         lead(digit, n = 2) == 1,
         lead(digit, n = 3) == 1,
         lead(digit, n = 4) == 0,
         lead(digit, n = 5) == 3)


# A tibble: 4 × 2
  digit_position digit
           <dbl> <dbl>
1          53673     0
2         237931     0
3         430480     0
4         912174     0




Code

title: Tidy Tuesday - Pi Digits
text:
Building the birthday lookup
temp above gives us every date in a (leap) year. From there we turn each date into a zero-padded MMDD string (bday), and do the same for every 4-digit window of \(\pi\)’s digits (vals4), so the two can be joined directly.


Code
pi_digits |>
  filter(digit == 1, lead(digit) == 1, lead(digit, n = 2) == 2,
         lead(digit, n = 3) == 9, lead(digit, n = 4) == 7,
         lead(digit, n = 5) == 3)


# A tibble: 0 × 2
# ℹ 2 variables: digit_position <dbl>, digit <dbl>


Code
library(lubridate)
library(latex2exp)
temp <- ymd("2000-01-01") + days(0:365)

head(data.frame(month = month(temp), day = day(temp)) |>
  mutate(month = ifelse(nchar(month) == 1, paste0("0", month), month),
         day = ifelse(nchar(day) == 1, paste0("0",day), day),
         bday = paste0(month, day)))


  month day bday
1    01  01 0101
2    01  02 0102
3    01  03 0103
4    01  04 0104
5    01  05 0105
6    01  06 0106


Code
bdays <- data.frame(month = month(temp), day = day(temp), temp) |>
  mutate(month = ifelse(nchar(month) == 1, paste0("0", month), month),
         day = ifelse(nchar(day) == 1, paste0("0",day), day),
         bday = paste0(month, day))


pi_days <- pi_digits |>
  mutate(vals4 = paste0(digit, lead(digit, n = 1), lead(digit, n = 2),
                        lead(digit, n = 3)))

join_days <- bdays |>
  left_join(pi_days, by = c("bday" = "vals4"))

join_days |>
  group_by(bday) |>
  summarize(num_bday = n())

title: Tidy Tuesday - Pi Digits
section: How many birthdays actually show up?
text:
How many birthdays actually show up?
Every one of the 366 possible dates turns out to occur somewhere in the first million digits of \(\pi\) - some many more times than others. The bar chart above already hints at this, but a polar layout makes it easier to see how the counts spread across the calendar. Each wedge is a date, coloured by month, and its length is how many times that date’s MMDD string appears in \(\pi\).


Code
join_days |>
  mutate(month_w = month(temp, label = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(x = bday, fill = month_w)) + #, color = "white" ) +
  coord_polar() +
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set3" )+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(fill = "", title = "Number of Birthdays Occurring in the first \nMillion Digits of pi") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = TeX("$\\pi$"), size = 47,
           color = "black", alpha = 0.5)









So yes - your birthday is (almost certainly) in \(\pi\), and probably more than once!

text:

library(tidyverse)

major_occupations <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-10-20/major_occupations.csv')
Shortening Labels
In order to group ridgeline plots by even broader categories than broad_field, and for the sake of legibility, we create field_short a shorter descriptor of each of the broad_fields. Since there are \(37\) unique broad_field entries, and time is money, I provided the output of unique(ai_salary_majors$broad_field) to ChatGPT, which provided me the re-naming labels, and also grouped each out these broad_fields into the broader categories, field_group.
Code
ai_salary_majors <- ai_salary_majors |> 
  mutate(
    field_short = case_when(
      broad_field == "Construction Trades" ~ "Construction",
      broad_field == "Visual and Performing Arts" ~ "Visual & Performing Arts",
      broad_field == "Precision Production" ~ "Manufacturing",
      broad_field == "Mechanic and Repair Technologies/Technicians" ~ "Mechanics & Repair",
      broad_field == "Transportation and Materials Moving" ~ "Transportation",
      broad_field == "Parks, Recreation, Leisure, Fitness, and Kinesiology" ~ "Sports & Recreation",
      broad_field == "Health Professions and Related Programs" ~ "Health Professions",
      broad_field == "Agricultural/Animal/Plant/Veterinary Science and Related Fields" ~ "Agriculture & Veterinary",
      broad_field == "Natural Resources and Conservation" ~ "Natural Resources",
      broad_field == "Culinary, Entertainment, and Personal Services" ~ "Culinary & Personal Services",
      broad_field == "Engineering/Engineering-Related Technologies/Technicians" ~ "Engineering Technology",
      broad_field == "Homeland Security, Law Enforcement, Firefighting and Related Protective Services" ~ "Protective Services",
      broad_field == "Communications Technologies/Technicians and Support Services" ~ "Communications Technology",
      broad_field == "Family and Consumer Sciences/Human Sciences" ~ "Family & Consumer Sciences",
      broad_field == "Military Technologies and Applied Sciences" ~ "Military Technology",
      broad_field == "Science Technologies/Technicians" ~ "Science Technology",
      broad_field == "Education" ~ "Education",
      broad_field == "Business, Management, Marketing, and Related Support Services" ~ "Business & Management",
      broad_field == "Engineering" ~ "Engineering",
      broad_field == "Computer and Information Sciences and Support Services" ~ "Computer Science & IT",
      broad_field == "Public Administration and Social Service Professions" ~ "Public & Social Services",
      broad_field == "Social Sciences" ~ "Social Sciences",
      broad_field == "Biological and Biomedical Sciences" ~ "Biological Sciences",
      broad_field == "History" ~ "History",
      broad_field == "Physical Sciences" ~ "Physical Sciences",
      broad_field == "Communication, Journalism, and Related Programs" ~ "Communication & Journalism",
      broad_field == "Multi/Interdisciplinary Studies" ~ "Interdisciplinary Studies",
      broad_field == "Architecture and Related Services" ~ "Architecture",
      broad_field == "Library Science" ~ "Library Science",
      broad_field == "Psychology" ~ "Psychology",
      broad_field == "Theology and Religious Vocations" ~ "Theology",
      broad_field == "Legal Professions and Studies" ~ "Legal Studies",
      broad_field == "English Language and Literature/Letters" ~ "English & Literature",
      broad_field == "Area, Ethnic, Cultural, Gender, and Group Studies" ~ "Cultural & Area Studies",
      broad_field == "Foreign Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics" ~ "Languages & Linguistics",
      broad_field == "Philosophy and Religious Studies" ~ "Philosophy & Religion",
      broad_field == "Mathematics and Statistics" ~ "Mathematics & Statistics",

    )
  )

ai_salary_majors <- ai_salary_majors |> 
  mutate(
    field_group = case_when(

      field_short %in% c(
        "Mathematics & Statistics",
        "Computer Science & IT",

        "Physical Sciences",
        "Science Technology"
